subtype: Approach: packing the finished work in the bag straight away [Action]

Zubin, across the aisle in the study hall, left his books in a heap, saying he'd pack in the morning. At 7:10 next day, the bus horn blew. Zubin was running between the study hall and the dorm, shouting, "Has anyone seen my science notebook?" Nirmala was already on the bus, bag on her lap.

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]

"Four days," he said out loud, counting on his fingers: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. He flipped through the textbook. Six chapters. His stomach dropped. Then he grabbed a pencil. "Six chapters, four days. That's... one and a half each." He wrote it on a sticky note: Mon, chapter 1 and half of 2. Tue, rest of 2 and chapter 3. Wed, 4 and half of 5. Thu, rest of 5 and 6. His friend Yosef texted: 'Studying?' Javier typed back: 'Only a chapter and a half today. Easy 👍'

qa.a: His stomach dropped, so he felt anxious, but after dividing them he felt confident enough to call today's share easy.

qa.a: Yosef may be surprised that Javier sounds so relaxed, and might want to know how the plan works.

grounding: Shows a child counting four days and six chapters and planning a chapter and a half each day, which makes the test feel doable.

subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]
passage: In the quiet corner of the school library, Sunaina opened her planner. Social Studies test on Monday. She counted the days she could study: Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Four. Then the chapters: Rivers, Soils, Crops, Minerals, Industries, Transport. Six. 'Six into four doesn't go,' she whispered. 'Unless... a chapter and a half each day.' She wrote it down, drawing a line through the middle of Soils and the middle of Industries. Bidisha leaned over. 'I'm doing it all on Sunday.' Sunaina pictured all six chapters squeezed into one day and shook her head. 'That's a mountain. Mine is four small hills.'

subtype: Approach: reading the chapter again and again [Action]
passage: My brother Santosh had a science test on Tuesday, so on Sunday he sat by the window with the chapter on light. I watched from my bed. He read it from start to end. Then again. Then a third time, lips moving a little. No pencil, no notes, nothing underlined. After the third time he shut the book and said, "Done. I know it all, every page looks familiar." Minakshi Aunty, who was visiting, asked, "Tell me, what is a shadow?" He opened his mouth, then said, "It's in the part with the torch picture." I can't say what he was thinking then, but he didn't open the book again.

qa.q: Which chapter did Santosh read?
qa.a: The chapter on light.

qa.q: What might Santosh have felt after the third reading?
qa.a: He seemed confident and relieved, saying every page looked familiar, even though he hadn't tried to recall anything.

qa.q: What else could Santosh try to check whether he really knows it?
qa.a: Close the book and answer questions like Minakshi Aunty's from memory, then check; recognising a page is not the same as recalling it.

qa.q: How might Minakshi Aunty see Santosh's answer about shadows?
qa.a: Minakshi Aunty hears him point to a picture instead of explaining, so she may suspect he recognises the page but can't yet explain it.

grounding: Shows a boy reading his science chapter three times without notes and feeling ready because it looks familiar, though he cannot recall it.

subtype: Approach: reading the chapter again and again [Action]

Wednesday. Hemant read the science chapter on magnets from the first line to the last. His highlighter lay capped beside him.
Thursday. He read it twice more, once after school and once after dinner. By the third time every diagram looked like an old friend. "I'm ready," he told his friend Santosh on the phone. "I've read it three times."
Friday. The first question asked him to name the two poles and say what happens when like poles meet. Hemant could picture the page, even the red-and-blue drawing in the corner, but the words wouldn't come. He stared at the fan, tapping his pen.

I'm writing so you know she did try, and that we will practise explaining out loud before the next test. Aditi (Ganga's mother)

subtype: Approach: feeling ready because the page looks familiar [Pitfall]

Sunday night
Science test tomorrow. I read photosynthesis this afternoon, twice, and closed the book feeling great. I could see the whole page in my head: the green leaf picture, the arrows, the sun in the corner. Then Ammi, folding clothes, said, "Afreen beti, tell me how a plant makes food." I said, "Sunlight... and the leaf... and then food." She waited. I couldn't remember what the leaf takes in, or what comes out. Hafsa giggled from the bed. I wanted to cry. It looked so familiar! Now I'm writing the steps on a card, one by one, and saying them out loud.

subtype: Approach: making questions and answering from memory [Thinking]
passage:
Thursday, 9 pm
Geography test tomorrow. Today I tried something new. I turned every heading into a question and wrote them on a page. 'What causes the seasons?' 'What makes day and night?' 'Why is it hot near the equator?' Then I shut the book and answered each one out loud to the wall. Hansa didi laughed from the doorway. 'Nitin bhai, are you teaching the wall?' Seasons: I said it was because the Earth goes nearer the sun in summer. I checked. Wrong! It's the tilt. So I read that part again, twice, and answered again. Now I know exactly which bit I didn't get.

qa.q: What did Nitin first say causes the seasons?
qa.a: Nitin said it was because the Earth goes nearer the sun in summer.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when the check showed the answer was wrong?
qa.a: Nitin seemed surprised but pleased, since the wrong answer showed exactly which part to study again.

qa.q: What could Nitin do with the questions tomorrow morning?
qa.a: Answer them all once more from memory before school, and re-read only the ones he gets wrong.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Nitin's method?
qa.a: Hansa finds it funny and teases Nitin about teaching the wall, without knowing how useful it is.

grounding: Shows a child turning headings into questions, answering aloud with the book closed, and using a wrong answer to see what to study again.

subtype: Approach: making questions and answering from memory [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: teaching the chapter to a younger sibling or toy [Action]
passage:
"Joel, sit. I'm the teacher now."
"Is this going to be long?"
"No. Water cycle. Mummy, can you hold the kettle?"
Mummy held the hot kettle by its handle, well away from Joel. Steam poured out.
"Step one: the sun heats the sea and water turns into vapour. That's the steam."
Maria held a cold steel glass upside down above it. Tiny drops formed.
"Step two: the vapour cools and becomes... clouds."
"How?" said Joel.
"It... condenses because... um." Maria stopped. "Wait. I don't know why it cools up there."
Mummy switched off the kettle. "Good. That's the page to read again."
Maria marked it with a star.
"Can I hold the glass next time?" Joel asked.

qa.q: What did Maria hold above the steam?
qa.a: A cold steel glass, upside down.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when she stopped at 'um'?
qa.a: She felt stuck and a little embarrassed, realising she didn't really understand why the vapour cools up high.

qa.q: What should Maria do with the starred page?
qa.a: Read that part again and explain it to Joel once more; the place she stumbled shows exactly what to study.

qa.q: How does Joel seem to experience the lesson?
qa.a: Joel starts off asking if it'll be long but ends up wanting to hold the glass, so he finds the steam demonstration interesting.

grounding: Shows a girl explaining the water cycle to her little brother with a steel glass and steam from a kettle her mother holds, and stumbling where her understanding is thin.

subtype: Approach: teaching the chapter to a younger sibling or toy [Action]
